newsitem.title: USA: McVeigh guilty of all counts in Oklahoma bombing.
newsitem.headline: McVeigh guilty of all counts in Oklahoma bombing.

text.p: Gulf War veteran Timothy McVeigh was convicted on Monday of blowing up a federal building in Oklahoma City two years ago, killing 168 people in a crime that stunned America.

The panel of seven men and five woman deliberated 23 hours over four days before finding McVeigh responsible for detonating a huge truck bomb outside the Alfred P. Murrah federal building on April 19, 1995.

They convicted him of all 11 federal charges against him, including conspiracy and the murders of eight federal agents. They reached their verdict after hearing five weeks of testimony and more than 160 witnesses in the emotional case.
The same jury will now decide, after hearing from more witnesses in a separate sentencing phase starting on Wednesday, whether McVeigh should be executed or spend his life in prison.
He sat impassively while the judge read the verdicts, with his elbows on a table and fingers laced in front of his face. He looked only at the judge throughout the verdicts.

Judge Richard Matsch had warned spectators that there could be no audible or visible reaction when the verdicts were read and victims' relatives in the courtroom sobbed almost silently as they listened, with tears streaming down their faces.
At the site of the bombing in Oklahoma City, hundreds of people cheered and wept with joy as they heard the verdict on television screens set up in the street.
"I'm extremely relieved. We've gone through an awful lot in the last 25 months and at least he is going through it now," said Bud Welch, who lost his 23-year-old daughter in the bombing.

Prosecutors said McVeigh, a decorated former soldier, parked a rented Ryder truck filled with explosives outside the building, occupied by hundreds of office workers and children at a day care centre. They said he was motivated by a raging hatred for the U. S government.

The powerful blast brought down nine stories of the concrete structure, crushing many victims inside and injuring hundreds of others. Nineteen children were among those killed in the worst mass murder in U.S. history.
The bombing horrified Americans and forever dispelled the notion that middle America was immune from such attacks.
This trial dealt only with the murder of the law enforcement agents in the blast. Oklahoma authorities plan to charge McVeigh separately with the other 160 deaths under state law.
Prosecutors described McVeigh as a "domestic terrorist" who blew up the federal building in an attempt to start the "second American revolution" and to see "blood flow in the streets of America."
They portrayed McVeigh as a good soldier turned bad and as a cowardly, cold-blooded killer who took out his anger on innocent men, women and children.

Defence lawyers maintained the government had arrested the wrong man and that the real killer could have died in the blast. They launched what would prove to be an unsuccessful onslaught on the FBI's work in the case, saying evidence- gathering was sloppy and that lab results linking McVeigh to the blast could have been contaminated.

Prosecutors said McVeigh bombed the building to avenge the deaths of about 80 Branch Davidian cult members in a confrontation with federal agents at Waco, Texas, two years earlier. A prosecution witness testified that McVeigh mistakenly believed that the orders for the Waco raid came from the federal building.

The prosecution presented evidence that he shopped for bomb components, rented the Ryder truck used in the bombing under a false name and that he had traces of explosives on his clothes when arrested after the blast. But it had no witness placing him in Oklahoma City on the day of the blast.
The defence maintained McVeigh was innocent and that an unidentified leg found in the rubble of the Murrah building may have belonged to the bomber.
McVeigh did not testify in his own defence.
The defence took aim at the credibility of Michael and Lori Fortier, key prosecution witnesses who testified that McVeigh, once their friend, had told them in advance of his plans for the bombing.
In Washington, President Bill Clinton said the end of the trial represented a "long overdue day" for the survivors and families of those who died. But he declined further comment.
